newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya defends return of controversial Moi aide.
newsitem.headline: Kenya defends return of controversial Moi aide.

text.p: Kenya on Friday condemned criticism of President Daniel arap Moi's cabinet reshuffle, which brought in a former Moi aide dropped from the cabinet five years ago amid corruption charges.
The reshuffle on Thursday sparked debate because of the return of controversial politician Nicholas Biwott, named as new minister in the presidency.
He had been dismissed in November 1991 after allegations of corruption and was also a suspect in the inquiry into the 1990 murder of popular former foreign minister, Robert Ouko.
Political analysts in Nairobi said Biwott's comeback was likely to upset western donors who underwrite lifeblood annual aid to the east African nation.

A government statement issued by Information and Broadcasting Minister Johnstone Makau singled out the British Broadcasting Corporation, the London-based Financial Times newspaper and the opposition for questioning Moi's move on Biwott.
"We take great exception to these negative reports and reactions and condemn them. Kenyans support the president for strengthening his cabinet team," Makau's statement said.
Makau hailed the return of Biwott, saying he was an experienced and competent person.

"Those criticising the reappointment of Biwott are the enemies of Kenya. They know Biwott is a very able minister and the foreigners and the opposition are jealous of his appointment," said the statement faxed to Reuters.

Biwott's position as industry minister in 1991 became untenable after British detective John Troon told a judicial inquiry into the Ouko murder that Biwott and late former security chief Hezekiah Oyugi were prime suspects.
Ouko's charred and mutilated body was found in February 1990 in a bush near his Kisumu home, a few days after he asked for an inquiry into high-level government corruption.
